claims.source: Within the MS, 21.0% of EC-projecting (EYFP+) neurons were triple immunopositive for PV, SATB1, and mGluR1a, while 37.1% showed no detectable signal for these three molecules (n = 62 tested neurons, six mice; Figure 1e,f).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunohistochemical data.

claims.claim: 37.1% of EC-projecting neurons within the MS showed no detectable signal for PV, SATB1, and mGluR1a.
claims.source: Within the MS, 21.0% of EC-projecting (EYFP+) neurons were triple immunopositive for PV, SATB1, and mGluR1a, while 37.1% showed no detectable signal for these three molecules (n = 62 tested neurons, six mice; Figure 1e,f).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunohistochemical data.

claims.claim: Neurons found nearby as PV+/SATB1+/mGluR1a– did not project to the EC, consistent with the profile of CA3-projecting Teevra cells.
claims.source: Neurons found nearby as PV+/SATB1+/mGluR1a– did not project to the EC (Figure 1f), consistent with the profile of CA3-projecting Teevra cells (Joshi et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data and comparison to a previous study.

claims.claim: Within the DB, 44.8% of neurons were only SATB1+ with the remainder of cells being triple immunonegative.
claims.source: Within the DB, 44.8% of neurons were only SATB1+ with the remainder of cells being triple immunonegative (n = 29 tested neurons, six mice).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunohistochemical data.

claims.claim: Only 2/13 tested EYFP+ neurons were ChAT+/PV–/mGluR1a–, 1/13 was only mGluR1a+, and 10/13 lacked detectable immunoreactivity (ChAT–/PV–/mGluR1a–).
claims.source: A subset of EYFP+ neurons were tested for choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) (Kondo and Zaborszky, 2016; Unal et al., 2015), PV and mGluR1a. Only 2/13 tested were ChAT+/PV–/mGluR1a–, 1/13 was only mGluR1a+, and 10/13 lacked detectable immunoreactivity (ChAT–/PV–/mGluR1a–).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunohistochemical data.

claims.claim: The PV– and ChAT– MSDB neurons probably comprise both GABAergic and glutamatergic EC-projecting neurons.
claims.source: The PV– and ChAT– MSDB neurons probably comprise both GABAergic and glutamatergic EC-projecting neurons (Fuchs et al., 2016; Gonzalez-Sulser et al., 2014; Justus et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the data and supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Eight labeled neurons had projection axons heading towards the EC via the dorsal fornix, with 5/8 forming thin collaterals and terminals within deep layers of the caudo-dorsal EC.
claims.source: To determine the temporal patterns of signals sent from the basal forebrain to the EC, we lowered glass electrodes into the MSDB in drug-free awake head-restrained mice to record neurons extracellularly, then visualized their axon collaterals and terminals in the cortex by juxtacellular labeling (Figure 2). Eight labeled neurons had projection axons heading towards the EC via the dorsal fornix, with 5/8 forming thin collaterals and terminals within deep layers of the caudo-dorsal EC (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Tables 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by anatomical data from juxtacellular labeling experiments.

claims.claim: All eight labeled neurons showed strong rhythmic burst firing occurring during both locomotion and immobility.
claims.source: Nevertheless, all eight neurons showed strong rhythmic burst firing occurring during both locomotion and immobility (Figures 2a,b,d,e and 3f,g), with longer bursts displaying accommodation (Figures 2a,b and 3f,g).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data from recordings.

claims.claim: Approximately 10% of bursts were >200 ms, and were often associated with high gamma power in hippocampal LFPs during immobility.
claims.source: Approximately 10% of bursts were >200 ms, and were often associated with high gamma power in hippocampal LFPs during immobility (Figures 2a,b and 3g) (Carr et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data and a citation to Carr et al., 2012.

claims.claim: All neurons were significantly coupled to theta oscillations, with 6/8 preferentially firing around the peak, and 2/8 on the descending phase.
claims.source: All neurons were significantly coupled to theta oscillations, with 6/8 preferentially firing around the peak, and 2/8 on the descending phase (p<0.0001 for all cells, Rayleigh test for uniformity; Figures 2a,b,f and 3f, Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phase coupling analysis of electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: Mid-gamma oscillations were coupled to theta cycles preferentially at the theta peak.
claims.source: As expected, mid-gamma oscillations were coupled to theta cycles preferentially at the theta peak (detected from CA1d LFPs of n = 7/8 animals with recorded septo-entorhinal neurons, Figure 2g).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of LFP data.

claims.claim: A subset of neurons preferentially coupled to the peak of mid-gamma oscillations.
claims.source: A subset of neurons preferentially coupled to the peak of mid-gamma oscillations (p<0.001 for n = 3/7 tested neurons, Rayleigh test; Figure 2h, Table 3), suggesting that theta-coupled septo-entorhinal neurons participate in entorhinal cortical gamma activity (Chrobak et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phase coupling analysis of electrophysiological data and a citation to Chrobak et al., 2000.

claims.claim: Single recorded and labeled EC-projecting neurons innervated multiple extra-hippocampal regions, with the majority of their terminals outside the EC located in the PrSd.
claims.source: As predicted by the viral tracing, single recorded and labeled EC-projecting neurons innervated multiple extra-hippocampal regions, with the majority of their terminals outside the EC located in the PrSd (Figures 3 and 4, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 4, Table 1, Figure 3—video 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by anatomical data from juxtacellular labeling experiments.

claims.claim: Extracellularly recorded EC-projecting neurons were immunopositive for PV (n = 8/8 tested cells), SATB1 (n = 6/6), and mGluR1a (n = 6/6), and their terminals were immunoreactive for VGAT (n = 2/2 tested cells).
claims.source: Extracellularly recorded EC-projecting neurons were immunopositive for PV (n = 8/8 tested cells), SATB1 (n = 6/6), and mGluR1a (n = 6/6), and their terminals were immunoreactive for VGAT (n = 2/2 tested cells; Figure 3b,d,e, Table 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunohistochemical data.

claims.claim: These GABAergic PV+ neurons are named 'orchid cells' based on shared cortical target regions, similarity in rhythmic burst firing patterns, strong theta coupling, overlapping molecular profiles, and the resemblance of the axon to Phalaenopsis orchids.
claims.source: Based on the shared cortical target regions (Table 1), similarity in rhythmic burst firing patterns (Figure 2a,b, Figure 3f,g; see below), strong theta coupling (Figure 2f), overlapping molecular profiles (Table 4), and the resemblance of the axon to Phalaenopsis orchids (Figure 3—figure supplement 5), we name these GABAergic PV+ neurons 'orchid cells'.
claims.evidence: This is a naming convention based on multiple lines of evidence from the study.

claims.claim: Orchid cells had 6.0 ± 1.8 primary dendrites extending from all axes.
claims.source: Orchid cells had 6.0 ± 1.8 primary dendrites (mean ±s.d., n = 4 cells) extending from all axes, which were similar to the distributions of CA3-projecting Teevra cell dendrites (Joshi et al., 2017) (χ2 = 0.02, p=0.8817, n = 4 orchid cells versus n = 4 Teevra cells).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative anatomical data and statistical comparison to Teevra cells.

claims.claim: PV+/SATB1+/mGluR1a + orchid cells provide rhythmic bursts of GABAergic input to specific extra-hippocampal regions of the temporal cortex.
claims.source: We conclude that PV+/SATB1+/mGluR1a + orchid cells provide rhythmic bursts of GABAergic input to specific extra-hippocampal regions of the temporal cortex.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the anatomical and physiological data presented.

claims.claim: Terminals of strongly-labeled orchid cell TV58g were observed in the fasciola cinereum (FC).
claims.source: To gain insight into the role of rhythmic GABAergic input from orchid cells to cortical circuits, we followed orchid-like collaterals to synaptic targets (Figures 3a and 4). Terminals of strongly-labeled orchid cell TV58g were observed in the fasciola cinereum (FC; marked by Amigo2 mRNA expression as in CA2) (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 4a,b, Table 5; see also Materials and Methods - Additional details of orchid cell projections) (Laeremans et al., 2013), followed more temporally by terminals in RSg layer 6 (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 2b); this region was also innervated by another cell (AJ50j, Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by anatomical data from juxtacellular labeling experiments.

claims.claim: No terminals of any orchid cell were observed in the hippocampus or dentate gyrus.
claims.source: Apart from the FC, no terminals of any orchid cell were observed in the hippocampus or dentate gyrus (n = 0/6 cells, Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by anatomical observations from juxtacellular labeling experiments.

claims.claim: TV58g extensively innervated caudo-dorsal EC (45.6% of cortical varicosities).
claims.source: The axon of TV58g subsequently extensively innervated caudo-dorsal EC (45.6% of cortical varicosities, Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Table 1) preferentially in layer 6 (expression of the Tmem178 gene; Figure 3—figure supplement 4c, Table 5); we observed terminals from three other orchid cells at a similar location (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative anatomical data from juxtacellular labeling experiments.

claims.claim: No terminals were observed in the Wfs1-expressing PaS region.
claims.source: No terminals were observed in the Wfs1-expressing PaS region (n = 0/6 cells; Table 1; Figure 3—figure supplement 4d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by anatomical observations from juxtacellular labeling experiments.

claims.claim: In the PrSd, 5/5 tested targets were PV+ and 3/7 tested were nNOS + interneurons, including 1 PV+ cell.
claims.source: We determined the molecular profiles of 13 targeted cortical neurons from the most strongly-labeled orchid cell (n = 1 neuron; Table 6) and used electron microscopy to test the reliability of predicting synaptic connections from light microscopy. In the PrSd, 5/5 tested targets were PV+ (Figure 4a,b) and 3/7 tested were nNOS + interneurons, including 1 PV+ cell (Table 6).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunohistochemical data.

claims.claim: In the electron microscopic study, all 11 tested boutons formed synapses with interneurons; 6 (55%) of them dendrites, and five somata.
claims.source: In the electron microscopic study (from the same orchid cell), all 11 tested boutons formed synapses with interneurons; 6 (55%) of them dendrites (Figure 4ci,ii), and five somata (Figure 4ciii), including a PV+/SATB1+/mGluR1a + interneuron (Figure 4b) receiving four synapses (Figure 4ci).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data.

claims.claim: Targets in three regions (PrSd, RSg and FC) were SATB1+ (n = 13/13), but CCK– (n = 0/10).
claims.source: Overall, somata and proximal dendrites of GABAergic interneurons received extensive innervation by orchid cell terminals (Figure 4b–f). Targets in three regions (PrSd, RSg and FC) were SATB1+ (n = 13/13; Figure 4b,e), but CCK– (n = 0/10) (Table 6).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunohistochemical data.

claims.claim: The axon showed target selectivity, as nearby interneurons with different molecular profiles were not targeted.
claims.source: The axon showed target selectively, as nearby interneurons with different molecular profiles were not targeted (Figure 4b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by anatomical observations.

claims.claim: Orchid cell axon terminals were apposed to some cortical neurons with high levels of endogenous biotin (n = 8/13 targets), suggesting that these are interneurons with high metabolic activity, such as 'fast spiking' neurons.
claims.source: We observed for four orchid cells that their axon terminals were apposed to some cortical neurons with high levels of endogenous biotin (e.g. Figure 4d; n = 8/13 targets, Table 6), suggesting that these are interneurons with high metabolic activity, such as 'fast spiking' neurons.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical observations and knowledge about endogenous biotin levels.

claims.claim: PV+ orchid cells influence extra-hippocampal regions via rhythmic modulation of select subpopulations of local GABAergic interneurons innervating them.
claims.source: These data, along with the preferential targets of PV+ MSDB axons in EC (Unal et al., 2015), suggest that PV+ orchid cells influence extra-hippocampal regions, via rhythmic modulation of select subpopulations of local GABAergic interneurons innervating them (Figure 4g).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data and supported by a citation to Unal et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Movement periods were detected by the combination of video, wheel activity and in some cases EMG or accelerometer.
claims.source: Movement periods were detected by the combination of video, wheel activity and in some cases EMG or accelerometer.
claims.evidence: This describes the methods used for behavioral state classification.

claims.claim: Four behavioral states were categorized: locomotion (LM); small movements (SM), which typically included postural shifts, limb and tail motion; spontaneous whisking and/or sniffing (WS) without other movements; and immobility (IM).
claims.source: We categorized four behavioral states in the head-restrained mouse: locomotion (LM); small movements (SM), which typically included postural shifts, limb and tail motion; spontaneous whisking and/or sniffing (WS) without other movements; and immobility (IM) (Table 7).
claims.evidence: This describes the behavioral state classification used in the study.

claims.claim: During LM and SM, theta oscillations dominated the CA1d LFP.
claims.source: During LM and SM, theta oscillations dominated the CA1d LFP (Figures 2a,b, 3f and 5a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by LFP data.

claims.claim: During WS and IM, LIA emerged in the hippocampus and more regular 'delta' 2–4 Hz oscillations were present in the MS.
claims.source: During WS and IM, LIA emerged in the hippocampus and more regular 'delta' 2–4 Hz oscillations were present in the MS (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a) (Fujisawa and Buzsáki, 2011; Nerad and McNaughton, 2006; Wolansky et al., 2006), often at higher power when the mouse was breathing more deeply.
claims.evidence: This is supported by LFP data and citations to Fujisawa and Buzsáki, 2011; Nerad and McNaughton, 2006; Wolansky et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Orchid cell rhythmicity was evident during all four behavioral states, with autocorrelograms exhibiting robust peaks and troughs.
claims.source: Orchid cell rhythmicity was evident during all four behavioral states, with autocorrelograms exhibiting robust peaks and troughs (Figure 2d,e, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: The peak in the autocorrelograms was at 143.8 ± 19.8 ms during locomotion but occurred later during the other states (SM: 169.6 ± 38.8 ms, n = 7; WS: 167.5 ± 18.6 ms, n = 6; IM: 174.4 ± 26.4 ms, n = 8).
claims.source: The peak in the autocorrelograms was at 143.8 ± 19.8 ms during locomotion (mean ±s.d., n = 8 cells) but occurred later during the other states (SM: 169.6 ± 38.8 ms, n = 7; WS: 167.5 ± 18.6 ms, n = 6; IM: 174.4 ± 26.4 ms, n = 8; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: Rhythmic firing was within the lower frequency range of 5–12 Hz theta oscillations (~80–200 ms) during all behavioral states, with cells exhibiting faster rhythmic firing patterns during locomotion when theta oscillations were at their highest frequency and power.
claims.source: Rhythmic firing was thus within the lower frequency range of 5–12 Hz theta oscillations (~80–200 ms) during all behavioral states, with cells exhibiting faster rhythmic firing patterns during locomotion when theta oscillations were at their highest frequency and power (Figure 5a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: 5/8 orchid cells increased firing close to the peak of the variable duration LIA cycles during CA1d LIA 'non-theta' periods, with bursts beginning on the rising phase.
claims.source: But when we tested for rhythmic burst firing during CA1d LIA (<5 Hz) 'non-theta' periods (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a), we found that 5/8 orchid cells increased firing close to the peak of the variable duration LIA cycles, with bursts beginning on the rising phase (neurons AJ44j, TV50a, TV58g, AJ50j, and MS19b; Figure 5b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of electrophysiological data during LIA periods.

claims.claim: Orchid cells can couple to irregular low frequency (<5 Hz) cortical activity in addition to 5–12 Hz theta oscillations.
claims.source: These data suggest that orchid cells can couple to irregular low frequency (<5 Hz) cortical activity in addition to 5–12 Hz theta oscillations.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the firing patterns observed during LIA periods.

claims.claim: The mean firing rates of orchid cells during locomotion were different than rates during immobility (mean ±s.d. 55.2 ± 14.1 Hz LM versus 39.8 ± 8.1 Hz IM; n = 8, t7 = 3.93, p=0.0057, paired t-test).
claims.source: In addition to behavioral state-dependent differences in rhythmic firing, the mean firing rates of orchid cells during locomotion were different than rates during immobility (mean ±s.d. 55.2 ± 14.1 Hz LM versus 39.8 ± 8.1 Hz IM; n = 8, t7 = 3.93, p=0.0057, paired t-test; Figure 5a,c, Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of electrophysiological data and statistical testing.

claims.claim: Putative orchid cells had different mean firing rates during locomotion and immobility (61.7 ± 18.0 Hz LM versus 43.4 ± 8.9 Hz IM; n = 8, t7 = 3.80, p=0.0067, paired t-test).
claims.source: We encountered other neurons (n = 7 unlabeled and n = 1 labeled PV+/SATB1+ mGluR1a + neuron) that matched the criteria and were classified as putative orchid cells (Figure 5d,f,g, Figure 5—figure supplement 1b, Tables 4, 8 and 9). These cells also had different mean firing rates during locomotion and immobility (61.7 ± 18.0 Hz LM versus 43.4 ± 8.9 Hz IM; n = 8, t7 = 3.80, p=0.0067, paired t-test; Table 8).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of electrophysiological data and statistical testing.

claims.claim: Most putative orchid cells showed a phase preference close to the peak of CA1d theta oscillations (group mean phase (circular mean ± circular s.d.): identified, 178.6° ± 39.1°, n = 8; putative, 183.3° ± 38.5°, n = 8; difference = 4.7°; p=0.8143, permutation test).
claims.source: As with the labeled neurons, most putative orchid cells showed a phase preference close to the peak of CA1d theta oscillations (group mean phase (circular mean ± circular s.d.): identified, 178.6° ± 39.1°, n = 8; putative, 183.3° ± 38.5°, n = 8; difference = 4.7°; p=0.8143, permutation test; Figure 5f, Tables 1 and 9).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phase coupling analysis and statistical testing.

claims.claim: Putative orchid cells were also coupled to mid-gamma oscillations, and like orchid cells maintained a peak phase preference (n = 3/8 tested neurons).
claims.source: Putative orchid cells were also coupled to mid-gamma oscillations, and like orchid cells maintained a peak phase preference (n = 3/8 tested neurons, Table 9).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phase coupling analysis.

claims.claim: Two additional cells (TV77q and TV78l) that had similar long bursts but a low burst incidence were SATB1 +but PV‒, projected via the fimbria and innervated the dentate gyrus and CA3.
claims.source: To test the reliability of our prediction of orchid cell identity by these signature firing patterns, we recorded then labeled two medial septal neurons that had similar long bursts (TV77q, median (and IQR), 69.0 (48.1) ms; TV78l, 86.3 (60.5) ms; Table 10) but a low burst incidence (TV77q, mean ± s.d., 1.5 ± 1.2 Hz; TV78l, 1.8 ± 1.2 Hz; Figure 5d). These two additional cells, which were SATB1 +but PV‒, projected via the fimbria and innervated the dentate gyrus and CA3 (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological and anatomical data from juxtacellular labeling experiments.

claims.claim: Teevra cells mostly exhibited short duration bursts during locomotion and preferentially fired at the trough of theta oscillations (group mean phase: identified orchid cells, 178.6°± 39.1°, n = 8; identified Teevra cells, 37.5°± 53.5°, n = 13; difference = 141.1°; p=0.0388).
claims.source: Another group of neurons, the Teevra cells, which target CA3 but not the dentate gyrus, are the most rhythmic neurons of the MSDB (Joshi et al., 2017), and thus had a high mean burst incidence (range LM 2.0–7.2 Hz and IM 1.1–5.8 Hz, n = 13 identified cells). However, in contrast to orchid cells, Teevra cells mostly exhibited short duration bursts during locomotion (Joshi et al., 2017) and preferentially fired at the trough of theta oscillations (group mean phase: identified orchid cells, 178.6°± 39.1°, n = 8; identified Teevra cells, 37.5°± 53.5°, n = 13; difference = 141.1°; p=0.0388; Figure 5f).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison to data from Joshi et al., 2017 and statistical testing.

claims.claim: No terminals of any septo-hippocampal neurons (n = 15 neurons) were observed in extra-hippocampal regions, indicating the reliability of our prediction of orchid cell firing characteristics.
claims.source: Overall, no terminals of any of these septo-hippocampal neurons (n = 15 neurons) were observed in extra-hippocampal regions, indicating the reliability of our prediction of orchid cell firing characteristics.
claims.evidence: This is supported by anatomical observations from juxtacellular labeling experiments.

claims.claim: During locomotion, theta oscillations dominated both CA1d and caudo-dorsal EC LFPs, with theta cycles in phase as in the rat.
claims.source: During locomotion, theta oscillations dominated both CA1d and caudo-dorsal EC LFPs, with theta cycles in phase as in the rat (Mizuseki et al., 2009) (Figure 6b,c,e).
claims.evidence: This is supported by LFP data and a citation to Mizuseki et al., 2009.

claims.claim: EC theta cycle troughs were significantly coupled to CA1d theta cycle troughs (p<0.001 for n = 4 mice (two sites per animal), Rayleigh test; circular mean ±circular s.d., 10.5 ± 15.8°, n = 4 mice (mean of 2 sites per animal)).
claims.source: Accordingly, EC theta cycle troughs were significantly coupled to CA1d theta cycle troughs (p<0.001 for n = 4 mice (two sites per animal), Rayleigh test; circular mean ±circular s.d., 10.5 ± 15.8°, n = 4 mice (mean of 2 sites per animal); Figure 6e).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phase coupling analysis and statistical testing.

claims.claim: During immobility, irregular LFP dynamics in the two structures showed similar activity, but the EC LFP lacked high-power ripples during hippocampal sharp waves.
claims.source: During immobility, irregular LFP dynamics in the two structures showed similar activity, but the EC LFP lacked high-power ripples during hippocampal sharp waves (Figure 6c) (Chrobak and Buzsáki, 1996).
claims.evidence: This is supported by LFP data and a citation to Chrobak and Buzsáki, 1996.

claims.claim: Medial septal neuron firing rate distributions during SWRs were different from a Poisson distribution (n = 4/4 orchid cells from four mice and n = 5 putative orchid cells from four mice; all p<0.05), with 4/9 neurons reducing their firing rate during SWRs.
claims.source: Medial septal neuron firing rate distributions during SWRs were different from a Poisson distribution (n = 4/4 orchid cells from four mice and n = 5 putative orchid cells from four mice; all p<0.05; Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Tables 3 and 9), with 4/9 neurons reducing their firing rate during SWRs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1d,g–i) (Borhegyi et al., 2004; Dragoi et al., 1999; Varga et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of firing rate data and citations to Borhegyi et al., 2004; Dragoi et al., 1999; Varga et al., 2008.

claims.claim: A transient firing rate increase was observed after ripples, which accounted for some of the bursts that were >200 ms in duration.
claims.source: Moreover, a transient firing rate increase was observed after ripples, which accounted for some of the bursts that were >200 ms in duration (Figures 2a,b and 3f, Figure 6—figure supplement 1a,b,d,g).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: Phase coupling to network oscillations by orchid cells, relative to CA1d, is maintained in the most caudal target region of the cells, the caudo-dorsal EC.
claims.source: These data suggest that phase coupling to network oscillations by orchid cells, relative to CA1d, is maintained in the most caudal target region of the cells, the caudo-dorsal EC.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the LFP data showing theta coupling between CA1d and EC.

claims.claim: The population of PV+/SATB1+/mGluR1a+ neurons within the MSDB was estimated to be 50,680 ± 2422 neurons (mean ± SEM, from 422 ± 35 counted neurons (mean ± s.d.), n = 3 mice).
claims.source: Finally, we estimated the number of MSDB neurons immunoreactive for combinations of PV, SATB1 and mGluR1a by a stereological method (Figure 7), to provide a baseline for all studies in mouse. We found that SATB1 could be used to delineate the borders of the entire MSDB (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a–c). We estimated the neuronal population containing at least one of the three molecules as 50,680 ± 2422 neurons (mean ± SEM, from 422 ± 35 counted neurons (mean ± s.d.), n = 3 mice, Figure 7—figure supplement 1d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by stereological counting data.

claims.claim: The largest group comprised PV–/SATB1+/mGluR1a– neurons (37.9 ± 2.5%), which were also the most numerous cells projecting to the EC.
claims.source: The largest group comprised PV–/SATB1+/mGluR1a– neurons (37.9 ± 2.5%, Figure 7b, Figure 7—figure supplement 1d), which were also the most numerous cells projecting to the EC (Figure 1f).
claims.evidence: This is supported by stereological counting data and viral tracing data.

claims.claim: Triple immunopositive neurons, which include the orchid cells, represented 7.2 ± 0.8% of the population.
claims.source: Triple immunopositive neurons, which include the orchid cells, represented 7.2 ± 0.8% of the population.
claims.evidence: This is supported by stereological counting data.

claims.claim: The proportion of PV+/SATB1+/mGluR1a + neurons was similar to PV+/SATB1+/mGluR1a‒ neurons (7.7 ± 0.5%), but no cell of the latter group was observed to project to the EC.
claims.source: The proportion of PV+/SATB1+/mGluR1a + neurons was similar to PV+/SATB1+/mGluR1a‒ neurons (7.7 ± 0.5%), but no cell of the latter group was observed to project to the EC (Figure 7b, Figure 7—figure supplement 1d, Figure 1f).
claims.evidence: This is supported by stereological counting data and viral tracing data.

claims.claim: Orchid cells, comprising <7% of the entire MSDB population of neurons immunoreactive for at least one of the three molecules, form a subpopulation of GABAergic neurons in the dorsal MS.
claims.source: We conclude that orchid cells, comprising <7% of the entire MSDB population of neurons immunoreactive for at least one of the three molecules, form a subpopulation of GABAergic neurons in the dorsal MS.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the stereological counting data.

claims.claim: Orchid cells provide rhythmic GABAergic input to target interneurons during both locomotion and immobility in distinct extra-hippocampal regions, primarily the PrSd and EC.
claims.source: They provide rhythmic GABAergic input to target interneurons during both locomotion and immobility in distinct extra-hippocampal regions, primarily the PrSd and EC (Figure 4g).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the anatomical and physiological data presented.

claims.claim: The observation of exclusively extra-hippocampal projecting GABAergic medial septal orchid cells innervating the caudo-dorsal EC reveals a specialized pathway that directly modulates extra-hippocampal circuits while bypassing the hippocampus.
claims.source: Our observation of exclusively extra-hippocampal projecting GABAergic medial septal orchid cells innervating the caudo-dorsal EC reveals a specialized pathway that directly modulates extra-hippocampal circuits while bypassing the hippocampus.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the anatomical data presented.

claims.claim: Orchid cells may correspond to the 'constitutively bursting' PV+ neurons with long burst durations and high intraburst frequencies identified in urethane-anesthetized rats.
claims.source: Orchid cells may correspond to the 'constitutively bursting' PV+ neurons with long burst durations and high intraburst frequencies identified in urethane-anesthetized rats (Borhegyi et al., 2004; Simon et al., 2006) (see also Type 1A cells in [Alonso et al., 1987; Gaztelu and Buño, 1982; King et al., 1998]).
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on comparison to previous studies.

claims.claim: Orchid cells represent a distinct subpopulation of Komal cells defined by their theta phase firing preferences and synaptic target regions.
claims.source: In contrast to Teevra cells, rhythmically bursting orchid cells, reported here, increase firing during locomotion, have long duration bursts, fire preferentially at the peak of CA1d theta oscillations, and innervate the PrSd and EC. Thus, orchid cells represent a distinct subpopulation of Komal cells defined by their theta phase firing preferences and synaptic target regions.

results.result: The manuscript establishes background knowledge about theta oscillations, spatial navigation circuits, GABAergic coordination, and MSDB projections to temporal cortex regions including the hippocampus, entorhinal cortex, and retrosplenial cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C28 represent established scientific knowledge supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These claims provide the necessary context for understanding the novel findings about orchid cells and are well-documented in the neuroscience literature.

results.result: Viral tracing experiments identified GABAergic MSDB neurons projecting to the entorhinal cortex, with 60.5% located in the rostral dorsal medial septum and extensive collaterals in extra-hippocampal regions, particularly the dorsal presubiculum (PrSd) and granular retrosplenial cortex (RSg), where 71% of terminals were VGAT-immunoreactive.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C37 are supported by quantitative viral tracing data with appropriate sample sizes (n=6 mice, 129 cells, 274 axons) and statistical analysis (p=1.6×10⁻⁷, Kruskal-Wallis test). The methodology using monosynaptically-restricted retrograde viral tracing is appropriate and well-described.

results.result: Immunohistochemical characterization revealed that 21% of EC-projecting neurons in the MS were triple immunopositive for PV, SATB1, and mGluR1a, while 37.1% showed no detectable signal for these markers. PV+/SATB1+/mGluR1a- neurons did not project to the EC, consistent with CA3-projecting Teevra cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C43 are supported by quantitative immunohistochemical data from 62 tested neurons across 6 mice. The comparison to Teevra cells (C40) is appropriately supported by citation to Joshi et al., 2017. The inference about PV-/ChAT- neurons (C43) is reasonable given the supporting citations.

results.result: Juxtacellular recording and labeling of eight EC-projecting neurons revealed strong rhythmic burst firing during both locomotion and immobility, with all neurons significantly coupled to theta oscillations (6/8 firing at the peak, 2/8 on the descending phase), and a subset (3/7) coupling to mid-gamma oscillations.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C49 are supported by electrophysiological recordings with appropriate statistical testing (Rayleigh test, p<0.0001 for all cells for theta coupling; p<0.001 for gamma coupling). The sample size of 8 labeled neurons is modest but appropriate for technically challenging juxtacellular labeling experiments in awake animals.

results.result: Single recorded and labeled EC-projecting neurons, named 'orchid cells', were PV+/SATB1+/mGluR1a+ GABAergic neurons with VGAT+ terminals that innervated multiple extra-hippocampal regions, primarily the PrSd, and had 6.0±1.8 primary dendrites similar to Teevra cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C54 are supported by anatomical and immunohistochemical data from juxtacellular labeling experiments (8/8 cells PV+, 6/6 SATB1+, 6/6 mGluR1a+, 2/2 VGAT+). The naming convention (C52) is justified by multiple converging lines of evidence. The dendritic comparison to Teevra cells includes appropriate statistical testing (χ²=0.02, p=0.8817).

results.result: Orchid cells showed selective targeting of extra-hippocampal regions with no terminals in hippocampus or dentate gyrus (except FC). Cell TV58g extensively innervated caudo-dorsal EC (45.6% of cortical varicosities) and PrSd. Electron microscopy confirmed synapses with interneurons (11/11 boutons), with targets being SATB1+ (13/13) but CCK- (0/10), including PV+ (5/5) and nNOS+ (3/7) interneurons in PrSd.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C64 are supported by detailed anatomical data from juxtacellular labeling and electron microscopy. The quantification is thorough (e.g., 45.6% of cortical varicosities in EC, 11/11 boutons forming synapses). The electron microscopy validation (C60) strengthens the light microscopy predictions. The target selectivity (C62) is demonstrated by the observation that nearby interneurons with different molecular profiles were not targeted.

results.result: Orchid cells exhibited rhythmic firing across four behavioral states (locomotion, small movements, whisking/sniffing, immobility), with autocorrelogram peaks at 143.8±19.8 ms during locomotion and longer intervals during other states. Five of eight orchid cells increased firing near the peak of LIA cycles during non-theta periods, suggesting coupling to irregular low-frequency (<5 Hz) cortical activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C73 are supported by quantitative analysis of electrophysiological data across multiple behavioral states with appropriate sample sizes (n=8 cells for most analyses, n=6-7 for some states). The behavioral state classification methods are clearly described (C65-C66). The inference about coupling to low-frequency activity (C73) is reasonable given the data showing firing at LIA peaks (C72).

results.result: Orchid cells showed significantly higher mean firing rates during locomotion versus immobility (55.2±14.1 Hz vs 39.8±8.1 Hz, p=0.0057, paired t-test). Putative orchid cells (n=8) showed similar properties. Two SATB1+/PV- neurons with long bursts but low burst incidence projected to dentate gyrus and CA3, not EC. Teevra cells (n=13) fired at theta trough, contrasting with orchid cells' theta peak firing (difference=141.1°, p=0.0388).
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C80 are supported by quantitative electrophysiological data with appropriate statistical testing (paired t-tests, permutation tests). The identification of putative orchid cells based on firing criteria (C75-C77) is validated by the negative control experiments (C78) showing that neurons with similar burst durations but different characteristics project elsewhere. The comparison to Teevra cells (C79) provides important context and is statistically significant.

results.result: During locomotion, theta oscillations in CA1d and caudo-dorsal EC were in phase (EC theta troughs coupled to CA1d troughs, p<0.001, circular mean 10.5±15.8°). During immobility, EC LFP lacked high-power ripples. Orchid cell firing rates during SWRs differed from Poisson distribution (9/9 cells, p<0.05), with 4/9 reducing firing and a transient increase observed after ripples.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C86 are supported by simultaneous LFP recordings from CA1d and EC in 4 mice with appropriate statistical testing (Rayleigh test for phase coupling, comparison to Poisson distribution for SWR firing). The anatomical verification of recording sites using juxtacellular labeling strengthens the localization claims. The inference about maintained phase coupling (C86) is reasonable given the data.

results.result: Stereological counting estimated 50,680±2422 PV+/SATB1+/mGluR1a+ neurons in the MSDB, with the largest group being PV-/SATB1+/mGluR1a- (37.9±2.5%). Triple immunopositive neurons (orchid cells) represented 7.2±0.8% of the population. PV+/SATB1+/mGluR1a- neurons (7.7±0.5%) did not project to EC. Orchid cells provide rhythmic GABAergic input to extra-hippocampal regions during locomotion and immobility.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C92 are supported by stereological counting data from 3 mice with low coefficients of error (0.05-0.06). The quantification provides important context for the proportion of orchid cells within the MSDB population. The conclusion about rhythmic GABAergic input (C92) is well-supported by the combined anatomical and physiological data presented throughout the manuscript.

results.result: The discovery of exclusively extra-hippocampal projecting orchid cells reveals a specialized pathway bypassing the hippocampus. Orchid cells may correspond to 'constitutively bursting' PV+ neurons in anesthetized rats and represent a distinct subpopulation of Komal cells. Their multi-area innervation likely supports spatially-modulated neurons including grid cells. Disinhibition of EC glutamatergic neurons by orchid cells around theta peak may facilitate transfer of temporal sequences to hippocampus.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C102 mix well-supported conclusions (C93, C95, C99) with speculative interpretations (C94, C97, C98, C100, C102). While the anatomical and physiological data strongly support the existence and properties of orchid cells, the functional implications and comparisons to prior studies in different species/conditions require additional experimental validation. The predictions about caudo-dorsal EC properties (C97-C98) and functional roles (C100, C102) are reasonable but speculative.

results.result: The manuscript proposes mechanistic hypotheses for how orchid cells coordinate cortical circuits through theta-nested gamma rhythmic inhibition. Two main hypotheses are presented: (1) orchid cells inhibit theta-trough firing interneurons leading to disinhibition at theta peak, and (2) orchid cells target theta-peak firing interneurons modulated at mid-gamma frequency. Orchid cells may also coordinate SWRs and offline replay of spatial memory traces.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C113 are primarily speculative hypotheses about functional mechanisms, appropriately identified as such in the text. While these hypotheses are grounded in the presented data and supported by relevant citations, they require direct experimental testing. The speculation is reasonable and provides a framework for future studies, but the mechanisms remain unproven.

results.result: Cortical targets of orchid cells included PV+ and nNOS+ interneurons, with some PV+ neurons also expressing nNOS in PrSd. The manuscript hypothesizes that postsynaptic targets will be strongly theta modulated and that orchid cells coordinate cortico-cortical neurons forming gamma-timescale assemblies involved in mnemonic processes representing sequential information.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C121 combine well-supported anatomical observations (C114-C116) with reasonable inferences and hypotheses (C117-C121). The anatomical data on target cell types is solid. The functional interpretations (C119-C121) are well-grounded in the anatomical and physiological data, though they represent conclusions drawn from the data rather than direct experimental tests of function. The speculation about theta cycle skipping (C118) is reasonable but requires validation.

results.result: Viral tracing experiments identified GABAergic projections from the medial septum to the entorhinal cortex, with collaterals preferentially innervating extra-hippocampal regions (PrSd and RSg) rather than the hippocampus. Quantification showed 71% of terminals were VGAT+ and axonal branches were substantially greater in PrSd/RSg compared to hippocampal regions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised major concerns about inadequate quantification in Figure 1 experiments (Essential revision #1), stating 'this experiment lacks adequate quantification' and that claims about sparse hippocampal collaterals and VGAT immunoreactivity were 'anecdotal and requires proper quantification.' They also requested clarification on where in the EC axons terminate, noting conflicting reports in the literature about layer specificity.

results.result: Molecular characterization of EC-projecting neurons showed 21% were triple immunopositive for PV, SATB1, and mGluR1a, while 37.1% showed no detectable signal for these markers. PV+/SATB1+/mGluR1a- neurons did not project to EC, consistent with CA3-projecting Teevra cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers requested better explanation of molecular marker significance (Essential revision #3), asking 'what does SATB1 immunoreactivity indicate in the medial septum with regard to cell classification?' and requesting clarification of which cell groups correspond to previously identified populations. The lack of clear explanation undermines confidence in the molecular characterization.

results.result: Eight juxtacellularly labeled neurons projecting to EC (orchid cells) exhibited rhythmic burst firing during locomotion and immobility, were immunopositive for PV/SATB1/mGluR1a, fired at theta peak, and coupled to mid-gamma oscillations. These cells innervated multiple extra-hippocampal regions, primarily PrSd.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised critical concerns about selection criteria and sampling (Essential revision #2), stating 'It is unclear how many neurons (and animals) were recorded in total' and 'how the 8 labeled neurons were selected.' They noted this 'could substantially affect how one interprets the data' and questioned whether the proportion matches expected values from viral tracing. The lack of transparency about total recordings and selection criteria prevents full evaluation of these findings.

results.result: Detailed anatomical analysis of orchid cell TV58g showed terminals in fasciola cinereum, RSg layer 6, and extensive innervation of caudo-dorsal EC (45.6% of cortical varicosities), with no terminals in hippocampus, dentate gyrus, or PaS region.
results.evaluation: Reviewers questioned what happened to the 3/8 neurons that did not form collaterals in EC (Essential revision #4), indicating incomplete reporting of anatomical data. This raises concerns about selective reporting and whether the described pattern is representative of all recorded neurons.

results.result: Synaptic targets of orchid cells in PrSd, RSg, and FC were characterized as PV+ and nNOS+ interneurons that were SATB1+ but CCK-. Electron microscopy confirmed synaptic connections, with all 11 tested boutons forming synapses with interneurons. The axon showed target selectivity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised concerns about sample size and quantification (Essential revisions #6, #7), noting the small number of characterized neurons (13 targets from 1 cell) and requesting clarification on how many mice were used. They stated 'proper quantification is needed' for claims about target selectivity, indicating the evidence was insufficient to draw strong conclusions.

results.result: Orchid cells exhibited rhythmic firing across all behavioral states (locomotion, small movements, whisking/sniffing, immobility) with state-dependent differences in firing rates and burst timing. Firing rates were higher during locomotion than immobility. Putative orchid cells showed similar properties.
results.evaluation: Reviewers found the description unclear (Essential revisions #9, #10), asking 'What exactly does the first peak refer to?' and 'what is meant by due to state-dependent features of the spike bursts?' The introduction of 8 additional putative orchid cells raised questions about false positive/negative rates (Essential revision #8), with reviewers asking 'when these criteria are applied to all neurons with recovered axons...how many meet the criteria and don't have EC projecting axons.' This indicates concerns about classification reliability.

results.result: Two additional SATB1+/PV- cells with long bursts but low burst incidence projected to dentate gyrus and CA3, not EC. Teevra cells exhibited short bursts and fired at theta trough, contrasting with orchid cells. No septo-hippocampal neurons (n=15) had terminals in extra-hippocampal regions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers found the description of these control experiments unclear (Essential revision #11), asking 'Which ones? Do the authors mean the 2 cells that are mentioned in this subsection?' This lack of clarity, combined with concerns about classification criteria raised in Essential revision #8, undermines confidence in the reliability of distinguishing orchid cells from other cell types.

results.result: During locomotion, theta oscillations in CA1d and EC were in phase. During immobility, EC lacked high-power ripples during hippocampal sharp waves. Orchid cells showed non-Poisson firing rate distributions during SWRs, with some reducing firing and others showing transient increases after ripples.
results.evaluation: Reviewers found Figure 6 experiments 'quite confusing' (Essential revision #15), questioning whether data came from only 1 mouse and whether the 9/9 neurons were from the same animal. They also questioned 'the point of these experiments' and how they go beyond previous work from the Buzsaki lab, indicating the novelty and interpretation of these findings were unclear.

results.result: Stereological analysis estimated the MSDB population immunoreactive for PV, SATB1, and/or mGluR1a as 50,680 neurons. The largest group was PV-/SATB1+/mGluR1a- (37.9%), which were also the most numerous EC-projecting cells. Triple immunopositive neurons (orchid cells) represented 7.2% of the population.
results.evaluation: Reviewers requested that Figure 7 data be more directly compared to cell labeling data (Essential revision #16), asking 'is the proportion of triple positive neurons similar to the proportion of orchid cells in the total population of recorded MS neurons?' and whether data could be normalized to total cell populations. This indicates the relationship between the stereological counts and the functionally characterized cells was not clearly established.

results.result: Four behavioral states were categorized (locomotion, small movements, whisking/sniffing, immobility) based on video, wheel activity, EMG, and accelerometer. Theta oscillations dominated during locomotion and small movements, while LIA and delta oscillations emerged during whisking/sniffing and immobility.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not raise concerns about the behavioral state classification methods or the characterization of network states. These methodological details appear to have been accepted without challenge.
